reference: Warm antibody hemolytic anemia is the most common form of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. It is defined by the presence of autoantibodies that attach to and destroy red blood cells at temperatures equal to or greater than normal body temperature. The disease is characterized by symptoms related to anemia, including fatigue, difficulty breathing, jaundice and dark urine. In severe disease, fever, chest pain, syncope or heart failure may occur. Hemolysis (the breakdown of red blood cells) occurs mainly in the spleen, so mild splenomegaly is relatively common. Treatment typically involves a corticosteroid like prednisone. In cases that don't respond to treatment, splenectomy may be considered. Chronic and severe disease may be treated with <PERSON> or immunosuppressive medications.

reference: Is genetic testing available for systemic scleroderma? Because systemic scleroderma is not caused by a mutation in any one specific gene, clinical genetic testing to confirm a diagnosis or identify a "carrier" is not currently available. Even if someone is known to carry a version of a gene that may make them susceptible to the condition, it does not mean they will definitely develop the condition. You can view a list of centers that may be involved in research projects on systemic scleroderma on Orphanet's Web site. You can also view a list of clinical trials involving people with systemic scleroderma on <URL>. People interested in learning more about genes and genetic testing for systemic scleroderma should speak with a genetics professional.

reference: What causes systemic scleroderma? The exact, underlying cause of systemic sclerosis is unknown. The cause appears to involve some injury to the cells that line blood vessels, resulting in excessive activation of dermal connective tissue cells, called fibroblasts. Fibroblasts normally produce collagen and other proteins. Build-up of collagen in the skin and other organs causes the signs and symptoms of the condition. It is suspected that scleroderma may develop from a variety of factors, which may include: Abnormal immune or inflammatory activity Genetic susceptibility: while no specific genes are thought to cause scleroderma, certain genes (or combination of genes) may increase a person's risk to be affected. However, the condition is not passed directly from parents to children. Environmental triggers: suspected triggers may include infections; injury; drugs (e.g. vitamin K, cocaine, penicillamine, appetite suppressants and some chemotherapeutic agents); and chemicals (e.g. silica, organic solvents, pesticides, aliphatic hydrocarbons and epoxy resin). Hormones: because women develop scleroderma more often than men, researchers suspect that hormones may play a role. However, the role of female hormones has not been proven. Widespread scleroderma can also occur in association with other autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus and polymyositis.
prediction: The cause of systemic sclerosis (SSc) remains unknown. Researchers believe that an abnormal immune system response may play a role in causing SSc. The body's immune system normally protects against foreign invaders such as bacteria and viruses by producing antibodies to fight them. In people with autoimmune disorders like SSc, however, the immune system produces autoantibodies - antibodies directed at parts of their own cells and tissues instead of foreign substances. These autoantigens can trigger inflammation throughout the body, which damages healthy tissue. It is unclear how this abnormal immune reaction leads to fibrosis, but researchers suspect it involves genetic factors, environmental triggers, and other abnormalities in the immune response. Environmental factors thought to contribute include viral infections, exposure to certain chemicals, and radiation. Viral infections have been linked to some cases of SSc; however, no specific virus has yet been identified. Some studies suggest that smoking increases the risk for developing SSc and worsens its course. Other research suggests that ultraviolet light from sunlight may also be involved. Scientists continue to study these potential causes in hopes of finding ways to prevent and treat SSc more effectively.

prediction: The signs and symptoms of systemic sclerosis (SSc) vary widely from person to person. The disease can affect any part of the body but most often affects connective tissue throughout the skin and internal organs such as the lungs, heart, digestive tract, kidneys, blood vessels, nerves, joints, muscles, eyes, and brain. SSc has two main types: limited cutaneous (<LOCATION>) and diffuse cutaneous. Limited cutaneous SSc usually begins with hardening of the fingers and toes, which may be accompanied by swelling. Diffuse cutaneous <LOCATION> involves more than half of the entire body surface area and typically starts on the face, hands, feet, arms, legs, chest, abdomen, back, neck, scalp, ears, nose, mouth, lips, eyelids, genitals, palms, soles, knees, elbows, shoulders, buttocks, and heels. In addition to these areas, it also commonly occurs on the nails, hair, mucous membranes, and other parts of the skin that normally have less collagen. Symptoms of both forms include Raynaud's phenomenon, an abnormal reaction of the small arteries in the extremities to cold temperatures; inflammation of the lining around the large arteries (perivasculitis); thickened veins called telangiectasias; and tightening of the soft tissues under the skin (fibrosis). Other common features of SSc include dryness of the mouth, throat, vagina, penis, urethra, anus, and rectum; joint pain and stiffness; fatigue; shortness of breath; weight loss; fever; low red blood cell count (anemia), leading to weakness and tiredness; and kidney failure. Some people develop pulmonary fibrosis, scarring of lung tissue that makes breathing difficult. Others get high blood pressure, especially if they have involvement of the major arteries. Heart problems associated with SSc range from mild arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat) to severe heart failure. Digestive issues related to SSc involve difficulty swallowing food because of narrowing of the esophagus (the tube connecting the mouth to the stomach) and constipation due to reduced motility of the intestines. Eye complications occur when scarred tissue develops between the layers of the eye wall causing blurred vision or double vision. instruction: What are the treatments for Syringoma ?
reference: How are syringomas treated? People with syringomas have a variety of treatment options, for example pulsed ablative laser (CO2 or erbium) or light electrocoagulation using a fine epilating needle. To learn more about these and other syringoma treatment options we recommend speaking with your healthcare provider.
prediction: Syringomas can be treated with surgery. The surgeon removes all of them at once to prevent recurrence. If they recur after removal, laser treatment may help reduce their number. In some cases, no treatment is needed because syringomas rarely cause problems. However, if they do become bothersome, other options include - cryotherapy (freezing) - electrocautery (burning tissue with an electric current) - photodynamic therapy (a light-sensitive drug that kills abnormal cells when exposed to specific wavelengths of light) - topical medications such as 5-fluorouracil cream These methods should be used cautiously on areas where skin cancer has been previously removed. They also have side effects including scarring, changes in pigmentation, and crusting. Some people choose to remove just one syrmingoma so it does not bother them. This method is called selective excision. It involves removing the affected area along with surrounding normal skin. A scar will remain but usually fades over time. People who want to avoid surgery often use cosmetic camouflage techniques to hide the scars. Other noninvasive procedures are being tested in clinical trials. Check with your doctor about taking part in a trial. For more information, visit the National Cancer Institute's website.

reference: Syndromic microphthalmia, type 3 is a rare condition that affects the eyes and other parts of the body. Babies with this condition are generally born without eyeballs (anophthalmia) or with eyes that are unusually small (microphthalmia). Both of these abnormalities can be associated with severe vision loss. Other signs and symptoms of syndromic microphthalmia, type 3 may include seizures, brain malformations, esophageal <LOCATION>, delayed motor development, learning disabilities, and sensorineural hearing loss. The condition is caused by changes (mutations) in the SOX2 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.
prediction: Syndromic Microphthalmia Type 3 is an inherited condition characterized by abnormally small eyes. The severity of this disorder varies widely among affected individuals; some have no vision loss while others may be blind. Affected people also typically have other physical features that distinguish them from one another. These include short stature, low-set ears with prominent lobes, a broad nose bridge, a flat nasal tip, a wide mouth, a cleft palate, a single palmar crease on both hands, and webbing between fingers or toes. Some affected individuals develop intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe. Other signs and symptoms can occur later in life including hearing problems, seizures, heart defects, kidney abnormalities, and abnormal development of bones and joints. In addition, about half of all affected males will experience infertility due to undescended testicles. This condition results from mutations in the <LOCATION> gene located on chromosome 17. It has been found to cause approximately 20 percent of cases of autosomal dominant congenital insensitivity to pain syndrome. Autosomal dominant means that just one copy of the altered gene in each cell leads to the condition. People who inherit these changes usually show more than one sign or symptom of syndromic MIM3. However, they often do not have any associated health issues beyond those described above. Researchers believe that most cases result from new mutations occurring within families rather than being passed down through generations. As such, there is likely little risk for siblings of someone diagnosed with this condition to develop it themselves. Genetic testing laboratories offer diagnostic tests for this condition but their availability depends upon where you live. You should consult your doctor if you think you might be at risk for having children with this disorder. Your doctor can refer you to a genetic counselor or clinic near you so he/she can help determine whether prenatal diagnosis would be appropriate based on how much risk exists for developing this condition yourself or passing it along to future offspring. Prenatal diagnosis involves performing certain procedures during pregnancy which allow parents-to-be to find out whether their fetus has an inherited disease before birth. There are two main types: amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS). Amniocentesis takes samples of fluid surrounding the baby's organs inside the womb using needles inserted into the abdomen after the mother has already gone through her first trimester period (<DATE_TIME>). CVS uses needles placed through the skin onto either side of the uterus to collect cells from tissue growing around the placenta called the chorion. Both methods carry risks such as miscarriage although they're generally considered safe when performed correctly under proper care facilities' supervision.
